title: The Pressure
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart opens with a colleague's list of more than thirty things a secondary English teacher 'has to do' and calls it devastating precisely because it is familiar, authentic and impossible. He argues that the list overwhelms perfectionist, task-oriented people who enter a profession carrying life-and-death weight, and that US teachers also have far more instructional hours than peers in high-performing systems such as Finland. Rather than blaming policy alone, he insists that teaching remains noble and that teachers must accept the list is not fixed and not every item on it is equal. His move is to reframe the response to overload as a set of deliberate decisions: set constraints, force space for thinking, and practise satisficing and intentional neglect. The piece ends by naming the decision as the real work, simple and hard at once, since no one is coming to tell teachers what to drop.
points: The post makes the teaching workload concrete with a long, relatable inventory of duties, which shows why good-faith teachers drown rather than blaming them for poor time management.

Stuart pairs the personal list with a structural point, that Finnish teachers average about 600 instructional hours a year against roughly 1,100 for American teachers, so the pressure is partly built into the system.
He holds two things together: policy and bureaucracy can be bad, yet the work itself is still good, so resignation and soul-loss are not the only options.
The prescribed response is to set constraints, protect thinking time, and practise satisficing and intentional neglect, because nobody else will shorten the list.
The closing line, 'we've just got to decide', locates the remedy in a teacher's own prioritisation rather than in waiting for relief from above.
quotes: Obviously, this is a devastating list — devastating because it's familiar and real and authentic, and devastating because it sets us up for impossible frustration.

The mental picture I'm left with is of a drowning person, who in response to their drowning is thrown several bowling balls. It is no wonder that fewer people are drawn to education these days (below, a graph depicting the decline of teaching certificates in my state). Why would I want to enter a line of work that appears to suck the souls right out of teachers?

The good news is that even though teaching does suck the souls out of many who enter the field, it doesn't have to. Certainly, we've got some messed up policies in the USA, and we've got some detached bureaucrats ensuring compliance rather than solving problems, and there are states and systems that practically write, “We devalue teachers,” on giant billboards along the highway.

I'm sold out on the goodness of teaching, but I refuse to let it suck out my soul. I refuse to act under a list like the one at the start of this post. Why? Because it's an impossible list, and not every item on it is created equal.

And so that becomes a part of the work in systems where the pressure is insanely high. We set constraints, we force space for thinking, we start practicing the precious arts of satisficing and intentional neglect.

At the end of the day, we live where we live (unless we move) and we teach where we teach (unless we make a change). So, once we're here, no one is going to give us more time, and probably no one is going to come and tell us what we should stop doing so that the list is doable. In this case, it's simple and hard at the same time: we've just got to decide.
